opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is a real challenge, and I think it's going to become one of the central methodological questions in the field. If a model can think for hours, days, or eventually weeks on a single problem, you can't just run a big benchmark suite at that budget and turn the evaluation around in a reasonable amount of time.

I think there are a few approaches. The first is to lean on scaling trends. If you measure performance at a range of smaller inference budgets, say a minute, ten minutes, an hour, you can often see a fairly smooth relationship between compute and accuracy. Then you extrapolate. That's similar to what people already do with training compute: you don't train the giant model blind, you fit curves on smaller runs and predict where the big one will land. You have to be careful, because these curves can bend or plateau, and extrapolation is always a bit of a leap of faith. But it gives you a principled starting point.

The second is to be much more selective about what you evaluate. If each data point is expensive, you can't afford a thousand easy questions. You want a small number of really hard, really informative problems, the kind where the answer tells you something meaningful about capability, ideally problems where we know the answer but that took humans a long time to solve.

The third is to look at intermediate signals rather than only the final answer. Is the model making progress? Is it finding useful lemmas, ruling out dead ends, getting closer to a solution? If you can measure that partway through, you don't always have to wait for the full run to learn something.

And honestly, part of it is just accepting that evaluation is going to get slower and more expensive. In games research we dealt with a version of this: when your bot is playing at a superhuman level, it takes a lot of hands or games to get statistically significant results, and you have to design your experiments around that. I think the field is going to have to develop that same kind of patience and rigor for long-horizon reasoning. The days of evaluating a model in an afternoon may be numbered for the most interesting capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response describes a fairly smooth relationship between compute and accuracy, but does not clearly state that performance improves as the inference budget increases.

r002.rationale: It proposes measuring performance at smaller inference budgets, fitting a trend, and extrapolating to predict performance at larger budgets.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because it's a real problem. If you believe that test-time compute is a major axis of scaling, then you want to know what happens when a model thinks for a week, or a month. But you can't actually run that experiment many times. You can't give a model a month on every problem in a benchmark and still iterate on your research at a reasonable pace.

So the way I think about it is, you look at trends. This is really the same thing people did with pretraining. Nobody trained a hundred models at the frontier scale to figure out what the scaling laws looked like. You trained a bunch of small models, you saw a clean trend, and you extrapolated. Inference compute works similarly. You can measure performance at one minute, ten minutes, an hour, and if you see a consistent log-linear improvement, you have decent evidence about what longer budgets would give you, even if you haven't tested them directly.

Now, you have to be careful about which problems you look at. If you evaluate on something that saturates, where the model gets ninety-five percent at ten minutes, you're not going to learn anything about what a week of thinking buys you. So you want problems that are hard enough that the model is still improving across the range you can measure. The harder and more open-ended the benchmark, the more informative it is about the long-budget regime.

The other thing I'd say is you can decompose the question. A model thinking for a week isn't just one long chain of thought. In practice it involves things like generating many candidate solutions, verifying them, backing up and trying different approaches. You can study each of those components at a smaller scale. How reliably does the model verify its own work? How much does it benefit from parallel samples versus a longer serial trajectory? Those measurements tell you a lot about whether the long-budget extrapolation is realistic or whether you'd hit a wall.

And honestly, part of the answer is that we did this with poker and with Diplomacy too. We had a sense from the trends at small scale that more search would keep helping, and when we actually ran the large-scale experiments, the trends mostly held. That's not a guarantee. The trends can break. But I'd rather bet on a clean trend from careful measurement than on intuition about what happens at a scale no one has tested.

r001.rationale: It describes consistent log-linear performance improvement as inference time increases from minutes to hours.

r002.rationale: It proposes extrapolating trends measured at smaller budgets to estimate results at longer, untested budgets.

astra-6.text:
I think you’d want to establish scaling laws for inference-time compute. You can evaluate a model at budgets you can actually afford—give it more time to think, measure how much its performance improves—and then see whether there’s a predictable trend that lets you extrapolate to larger budgets.

The tricky part is that you need problems that remain meaningful as you scale. If the model already gets everything right with a minute of thinking, that benchmark tells you very little about what happens with an hour or a day. And you have to distinguish between the model genuinely making progress and just producing more tokens.

So I’d test the extrapolation at smaller scales first: use the cheaper runs to predict the more expensive runs, then check whether those predictions hold. That wouldn’t prove what happens at a budget you can’t test, but it would give you a more grounded estimate. I’d still want a few very expensive runs to check that the trend isn’t breaking down.

r001.rationale: It says to measure how performance improves as the model gets more time to think, indicating gradual gains with increased inference compute.

r002.rationale: It proposes using cheaper, smaller-budget runs to predict results at larger budgets that cannot be tested directly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you can approach this a bit like scaling laws for training. You don’t run every possible training compute budget before deciding whether to do a big training run. You measure performance at smaller scales and try to predict what happens at larger scales.

For inference, you could evaluate a model at a range of budgets—say, progressively more time spent thinking—and see whether there’s a predictable relationship between compute and performance. Then you can try to extrapolate beyond what you can conveniently test directly.

The tricky part is that the curve might flatten out. If the model keeps pursuing the same wrong idea, giving it more time may not help. So you’d want to validate those predictions at budgets you can actually measure, and look at whether the model is making productive use of additional compute. But I think developing reliable inference scaling laws would be a very useful way to reason about those much larger budgets.

r001.rationale: The response suggests measuring performance across increasing inference budgets, but does not clearly state that performance improves gradually as the budget increases; it says the relationship may flatten or additional time may not help.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly proposes measuring performance at smaller budgets and extrapolating beyond what can be conveniently tested directly.
